passage: Ganga arrived at school laughing at a video with her friends, so loud that the teacher, Farhan, looked over. By second period she was snapping at her desk partner for tapping a pen. After lunch she sat with her head down, and when Farhan asked whether she had finished the worksheet, her eyes filled and she whispered, "I can't do anything right." Fifteen minutes later she was giggling at a joke in the corridor. Farhan didn't remark on the swings or call her dramatic. He put a glass of water on her desk and said, "Take your time." Later he asked quietly whether she had been sleeping enough, and mentioned that the school counsellor was always around if she wanted a chat.

qa.q: What did Farhan put on Ganga's desk?
qa.a: He put a glass of water on her desk.

qa.q: What might Ganga be feeling as her mood moves from laughing to snapping to tearful?
qa.a: Her feelings may truly be shifting, from playful to irritated to discouraged within a few hours, and she may not understand why herself.

qa.q: How did Farhan support Ganga?
qa.a: He stayed calm and consistent, offered water, asked gently about sleep, and mentioned the counsellor, without calling her dramatic.

qa.q: How might Ganga's classmates experience her changing moods?
qa.a: They may find it confusing, like the desk partner who was snapped at, unless they remember that moods can swing a lot at her age.

grounding: A teen swings from laughing to irritable to tearful within hours, and patient consistency and gentle talk help.

passage:
Dear Anand bhaiya,
Sorry about how I've been at home. I know at breakfast I was laughing at everything, at lunch I snapped at you for taking the remote, and by night I was crying over a song I've heard fifty times. It's not you and I don't fully know why it happens. It just changes fast, like weather. Mummy says it's part of growing up, and I'm trying to sleep at a proper time because that seems to make it better. What helps most is when you don't make a big deal, and just say something normal or sit with me. Please keep doing that. I'll try to tell you when I need space.
Tarun

qa.q: What did Tarun snap at Anand for?
qa.a: Tarun snapped at Anand for taking the remote.

qa.q: What does Tarun feel about the mood changes?
qa.a: Tarun feels puzzled and sorry, since it isn't about Anand and Tarun doesn't fully know why the mood changes as fast as weather.

qa.q: What does Tarun say helps most?
qa.a: Tarun says it helps when Anand doesn't make a big deal and just says something normal or sits nearby.

qa.q: How might Anand feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and understood, since he learns the snapping wasn't personal and knows how to help.

grounding: A teen swings between laughing, irritable and tearful within a day, and calm consistency and gentle talk support balance.

passage:
Ankita, you asked on this podcast about being fourteen. Okay, I'm Gautam, and fourteen was a rollercoaster.
One evening I remember clearly. At six I was laughing so hard at a video my little sister sent that I fell off the bed. By six-thirty I was snapping at my mother because she asked if I'd done my homework. By seven I was crying in the bathroom, and I honestly couldn't tell you why.
My mother didn't shout back or say, "What's wrong with you?" She just stayed the same. Calm. Dinner at eight. Lights off by eleven, phones out of rooms. She'd knock and say, "Want to talk, or want tea?"
It drove me mad then. Now I think it saved me. I was sleeping about five hours before that. With proper sleep, the swings got smaller.
And when I did want to talk, she was right there, same as always.

qa.q: What time did Gautam's mother set for lights off?
qa.a: Lights off by eleven, phones out of rooms.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling that evening at fourteen?
qa.a: Gautam swung from amused to irritable to tearful within an hour, confused about why the moods changed so fast.

qa.q: What helped Gautam's mood swings settle?
qa.a: The mother's calm, consistent routine, proper sleep, and her gentle, repeated offers to talk or have tea.

qa.q: How might Gautam's mother have felt during those evenings?
qa.a: She was probably worried and sometimes hurt by Gautam's snapping, but chose to stay steady rather than react.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager's quickly changing moods, and patient consistency, sleep and gentle talk supporting balance.

passage:
I'm Pankaj, Chetan's older brother. On Friday I watched him go through what felt like five moods in an hour.
At dinner he was cracking jokes and doing impressions of his science teacher. Twenty minutes later, when Papa asked him to clear the plates, he slammed a glass down and shouted, "Why is it always me?" Then, by nine, I found him sitting on the terrace steps, eyes red, not saying anything.
I couldn't tell what was going on. Was he tired? Sad? Angry? Maybe all of it.
I didn't lecture. I sat on the step below him and said, "Long day?"
He shrugged. After a while he said, "I've been sleeping at two every night. Gaming. And I feel weird all the time."
"That'd make anyone swing about."
We made a deal: phone charges in the kitchen from eleven. I'd do the same. Sunday, he was just grumpy in normal amounts.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj find Chetan by nine?
qa.a: Sitting on the terrace steps, eyes red.

qa.q: What was behind Chetan's quick changes in mood?
qa.a: Chetan felt tired and out of balance after sleeping at two every night, which left him swinging from playful to irritable to tearful.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed calm and patient, sat with Chetan without lecturing, and made a shared deal about sleep and phones.

qa.q: How might Papa have read Chetan's outburst at dinner?
qa.a: Papa might have seen it as rudeness or laziness, not knowing it was linked to exhaustion.

grounding: An older brother's account shows a teenager's changing moods within an hour, and patience, sleep and gentle talk supporting balance.

passage:
Monday: At lunch Lalremsiami laughed so hard at Tejas's joke that she snorted milk. Ten minutes later, when he borrowed her pen without asking, she snapped, "Can you not?" and turned away. Tejas blinked, confused.
Wednesday: In the library, Tejas found her quietly crying over a history worksheet. He sat down next to her. "Do you want to talk, or should I just sit here?"
"Sit," she said. After a while: "I don't even know why I'm crying. I'm so tired. I've been staying up worrying about the exams."
Tejas didn't push. He brought her a biscuit from his bag.
Saturday: Lalremsiami messaged him: "Sorry for being all over the place this week. Slept nine hours last night. Feel human again."
Tejas replied, "No worries. Same time Monday for lunch? No pen stealing, I promise."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami snort at lunch on Monday?
qa.a: She snorted milk.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling in the library on Wednesday?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt sad and exhausted, crying without knowing why, after staying up worrying about exams.

qa.q: What made Tejas's support steady?
qa.a: He stayed patient and consistent, offering to talk or just sit, not pushing, and not taking her Monday snap personally.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when she snapped on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably confused and a little hurt, since she had been laughing only minutes before.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager's mood swinging from laughter to irritation to tears, and patient consistency and sleep restoring balance.

passage: Yogesh beta, you think your mother never slammed a door? Sit, and let your Hansa Nani tell you about Meena at fifteen. One Sunday she laughed so hard at your Nana's joke about the goat that she fell off the charpai. Twenty minutes later she was snapping at me because I had moved her bangles. By lunch she was crying over something she couldn't even name, face in the pillow. I wanted to shout, "Which Meena am I talking to?" Your Nana stopped me. He said, "She's tired. She was up reading till two again." So we tried something. No arguments after dinner, lights out at ten for everyone, even your Nana with his radio. And every evening I sat on her bed for five minutes, not asking anything, just there. The storms didn't stop. But they got smaller, and she started telling me about them. Now you slam doors, and she's the one sitting on your bed. That's how it goes.

qa.q: What did Meena laugh at that Sunday?
qa.a: Meena laughed at Nana's joke about the goat.

qa.q: What might young Meena have been feeling across that Sunday?
qa.a: Meena swung from amusement to irritation to a sadness she couldn't name, likely made worse by tiredness from reading till two.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Meena's moods settle?
qa.a: The family chose calm routines, no arguments after dinner and lights out at ten, and Hansa sat quietly on Meena's bed each evening, which made the storms smaller.

qa.q: What did Nana see that Hansa didn't at first?
qa.a: Nana saw tiredness from late-night reading behind the swings, so he stopped Hansa from shouting.

grounding: It shows a teenager swinging from laughing to irritable to tearful within hours, and patient consistency, sleep and gentle presence supporting balance.
